questions.q: Define "organic imagery" and give one example from Manjula's description of her sister Malini's illness in the play.
questions.a: Organic imagery describes internal bodily sensations (hunger, thirst, nausea, pain, fatigue). In the play, Manjula says Malini's "nervous system was damaged. Completely dysfunctional" and "a series of operations... reduced her existence to misery" — this evokes the visceral, organic sensation of chronic physical suffering. A wrong answer (e.g., quoting "wheel-chair" as organic imagery) reveals confusion between *tactile* imagery (external touch) and *organic* imagery (internal body feeling).

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the metaphor "The River Has No Memories" (the novel's title) functions differently from a simile like "The river is like a person with no memories."
questions.a: A metaphor ("X *is* Y") fuses the two identities, forcing the reader to perceive the river *as* an amnesiac entity — suggesting history, trauma, and language itself can be erased. A simile ("X *is like* Y") keeps them separate, allowing intellectual distance. The metaphor implies the novel *enacts* the erasure of Kannada memory by writing in English; the simile would merely *observe* it. A wrong answer that treats them as interchangeable misses the ontological violence inherent in metaphor — the very violence the play critiques.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "visual imagery cluster" to the TV studio setting in the opening stage directions. List three visual images and explain how they collectively establish the theme of technological alienation.
questions.a: Three visual images: (1) "big plasma screen", (2) "television sets, with screens of varying sizes", (3) "small red bulb". Together they create a cluster of glowing, mechanical eyes — impersonal, multiplying, watching. The "plasma" screen suggests bloodless modernity; "varying sizes" implies fragmentation; the "red bulb" is a cold, unblinking recorder. A wrong answer listing random props (chair, table, mike) without clustering by visual quality or linking to alienation shows inability to synthesize imagery into thematic patterns.

questions.q: Analyse how the extended metaphor of "the Image on the screen" operates as both a technological artifact and a psychological doppelgänger. Use two specific exchanges between Manjula and the Image.
questions.a: Technologically, the Image is a broadcast signal — "If the camera were on, I would be standing up too." Psychologically, it knows Manjula's secrets: "That bit about your sister Malini... the tears... could have been played down." The metaphor merges *external surveillance* (media) with *internal surveillance* (conscience). When the Image says "Me? You," it collapses the distinction between public persona and private self. A wrong answer that treats the Image only as a "ghost" or only as a "glitch" fails to hold the dual register — the central dramatic tension of the play.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the auditory imagery in Manjula's line: "Testing, Testing, One, Two, Three, Four, Five, Hello, Hello!" compared to the silence when she taps the mike and gets "No response." Which creates greater dramatic tension and why?
questions.a: The *silence* creates greater tension. The counting imagery establishes routine, professional control — "I have timed it." The sudden absence of expected auditory feedback ("No response") violates the sensory contract, mirroring Manjula's loss of control over her narrative. The counting is *predictable* sound; the silence is *shocking* sound. A wrong answer choosing the counting because "it's more descriptive" confuses quantity of imagery with dramatic function — tension arises from sensory *disruption*, not sensory abundance.

questions.q: Create a new metaphor that Manjula might use to describe her relationship with English, consistent with her voice in the play. Explain the source and target domains and the quality transferred.
questions.a: Example: "English is a polished mirror — it shows me a version of myself the world applauds, but I cannot recognize the face." Source: polished mirror. Target: English language. Quality transferred: *reflective distortion* — it reflects reality but alters it, creating a pleasing but alien image. A poor answer like "English is a thief" (simile-like, clichéd, no sensory ground) fails to meet the play's standard of metaphors that are intellectually precise, personally resonant, and linguistically self-aware.
